--- title: "[Graph.add_complete_bipartite_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a complete bipartite graph K(n1, n2) to the current graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L5139-L5244){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_complete_bipartite_graph( n1, n2, type=None, label=True, rel=None, part_attr="part", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Complete bipartite graph](/assets/graphs/add-complete-bipartite-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three complete bipartite graphs side by side for sizes 2 and 2, 2 and 3, and 3 and 4. The first part sits in a top row in the accent color and the second in a teal bottom row; every top node is joined to every bottom node and no two nodes in the same row are joined, giving 4, 6, and 12 edges." width="100%"} Creates two groups of nodes, `n1` in the first and `n2` in the second, and joins every node of the first group to every node of the second. No edges run inside a group, so the graph has `n1 + n2` nodes and `n1 * n2` edges and is bipartite by construction. Each node's group is stored in the `part_attr=` node attribute (`0` for the first group, `1` for the second), so the two sides can be recovered later. The first group is created first, then the second. In a directed graph every edge points from the first group to the second. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Complete bipartite graphs are useful for: - modeling two-sided systems where every member of one side relates to every member of the other (all customers and all products, all workers and all shifts) - test cases for bipartite algorithms such as matching, projection, and bipartite centrality, where the answers are known - building blocks in graph theory: `K(1, n)` is a star and `K(3, 3)` is one of the two minimal non-planar graphs ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n1]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes in the first group. Must be non-negative. [n2]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes in the second group. Must be non-negative. If either group is empty the result is a set of isolated nodes. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string (so `"1"`, `"2"`, ... in an empty graph); a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. [part_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["part"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute that records each node's group (`0` or `1`). Default is `"part"`. Pass `None` to skip storing it. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n1=` or `n2=` is negative. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} `K(2, 3)` has `2 + 3 = 5` nodes and `2 * 3 = 6` edges: ::: {#34f1d642 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_complete_bipartite_graph(n1=2, n2=3) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (5, 6) ``` ::: ::: The `part` column records which side each node is on. Nodes on the first side have one neighbor for every node of the second side, and vice versa: ::: {#77a78137 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_node_df().select("label", "part", "degree") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 3)
labelpartdegree
stri64i64
"1"03
"2"03
"3"12
"4"12
"5"12
``` ::: ::: `K(3, 3)` is bipartite but not planar: ::: {#8fef9f0c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} utility = ec.Graph().add_complete_bipartite_graph(n1=3, n2=3) utility.is_bipartite(), utility.is_planar() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
